blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Can I just alert my Lord to the fact that the next witness, who's Sophie Ellis, has this morning asked for a particular measure and a statement is being taken, so we'll just need a short break after this witness, please, if that's convenient to the court.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Certainly, yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: (In the presence of the jury)
My Lord, I will recall (sic) Joanne Williams, please.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: MRS JOANNE WILLIAMS (affirmed)
Examination-in-chief by MR ASTBURY

Nurse Williams, you given evidence already in this case so we know that you were, you are, a band 6 neonatal practitioner and that in June of 2015, you were employed in that capacity at the Countess of Chester Hospital in the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: I want to ask you, please, about a shift, a day shift, that you completed on Saturday, 13 June 2015. Do you recall that shift?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I do.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Do you recall coming on duty that morning?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: I know you have done this before, but you need to keep...
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: (Pause)
I do apologise.
I'm absolutely sure we haven't seen Ms Williams before.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: No, I was a little puzzled, but I didn't want to say anything in case it was me that was wrong.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I do apologise. If we start again.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Let's start again. We haven't seen you before.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I think we may have heard a statement read, that's why, and I apologise (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's the point: we have heard evidence from you, but it was agreed evidence and that part of the statement or that statement was read, but we've now moved on.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: If I can use this opportunity as well to urge you, please, I know it's a little bit odd, I'm asking the questions, not very good questions so far, but if you can direct your answers, please, to the ladies and gentlemen on the jury, they're the most important, so they can hear you. There's also people behind the screen, so we need to keep your voice up, please, if at all possible.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Let's start again. Can we begin with your full name, please?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Joanne Williams.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: And your profession, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Neonatal practitioner.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Am I right that you were employed in the Countess of Chester Hospital in June 2015?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: What was your status during that particular time?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I was band 6.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Thank you. We've heard a little bit about the various bands. Are there differences within even band 6 as a neonatal nurse?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Obviously as a newly qualified nurse you come in as a band 5 and then, as the progression in your career, band 6.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: So it's possible to progress even within band 6?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You can be a band 7.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think the question was: can you progress within band 6? You were band 5, you progress to band 6, but is there any difference between one band 6 nurse or neonatal practitioner and another?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It can be with qualifications.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: So you can get some additional qualifications?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: And then you can go on to become band 7?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: How long had you been a band 6 in 2015?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Can you remember?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: No (inaudible).
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Well, I want to ask you, please, more importantly about the events of that particular day. What time would your shift start on a day shift?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Half 7.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: And do you recall who you were allocated to look after that particular day?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, [Baby C].
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Thank you. Again, if you can keep your voice up, please. I know it's difficult.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We've heard already a little bit about the process when a shift begins where the staff come together, there is a general huddle, I think we've heard it described as, and then a handover at the bedside for your specific baby.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Was that the process as you recall it on the morning of 13 June 2015?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: From what I remember, yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Do you recall, please, where [Baby C] was situated in the unit when you came on duty?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. In nursery 1, the left-hand side, towards the sink, the bottom space, the intensive care space.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: We've seen some video footage of the unit and room 1 certainly has two doors right and left. Does that help you orientate you where he was?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The left-hand side.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Okay. Do you recall whether there were any other babies in room 1 on that morning?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't. I don't recall.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Okay. Do you recall whether the unit was busy that particular morning?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It doesn't particularly stand out that it was busy.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: We have the benefit of the notes that you would have completed during the course of your shift. And what I'd like to do, please, is to take you to those notes because I'm going to
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: ask you some questions about events that happened during the course of that day shift involving [Baby C]. So if I can ask Mr Murphy, please, to go to tile number 69 on the relevant presentation.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Before we click into the notes on that particular day, had you cared for [Baby C] in the days before this particular shift?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I think -- I believe so.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: All right. What did you know of [Baby C] generally at the time that you came on duty that morning?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That he was a baby born at 30 weeks, he was a small baby, small for gestation, and that's...
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Okay. All right. Did you know something of the circumstances of his gestation and birth?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That antenatally there was absent end-diastolic flow.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: And we've heard that his weight, do you recall, what his weight was at the time he was born?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: 800 grams.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: So let's go to your note then please, if we may. If we can click into it, Mr Murphy, and click behind it into the source material.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If we could enlarge the relevant section, thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's quite a detailed note and we can see it was written in retrospect, am I right, if we look at the top line at 4.19 that afternoon. So the notes may cover most of the shift, certainly up to that point. Could we go through it bit by bit and if I pause and take you to something else please bear with me, but I'll use this I hope to assist:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Care taken over at 8 o'clock."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That presumably would have been after this handover at the bedside or cot side that we've heard about?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: And you have noted:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Emergency equipment and fluids checked."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is that a routine for a nurse in your position?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, it is.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: You indicate that he's nursed on -- I think that's nasal CPAP; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Pressures between 4 and 5 centimetres in 23-26% oxygen?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: We've heard air contains 21% oxygen, so does that level of 23 to 26 tell you anything about his condition at that point?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It was a minimal requirement of oxygen to maintain his saturations.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Is that a good sign or a bad sign?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's a good sign.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: "CBG taken at 9 am."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: CBG, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Capillary blood gas.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: And it says:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Very good."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: What are you referring to there if it's not --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That it's in the normal parameters that we'd expect.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Right, okay:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "However, [Baby C] very unsettled and fractious."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Can you tell us a little bit about that, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: He was very unsettled in the morning. I remember him being very fractious, and that's not uncommon for a baby of his size necessarily. And he was -- he was unsettled. I've documented to say that he was unsettled.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Okay. The next note is:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "After discussion with Registrar Ogden on the ward round, [Baby C] taken off CPAP while out having skin-to-skin with mummy."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Just tell us about that, please, if you remember.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, I know obviously skin-to-skin is extremely powerful for any baby because obviously being next to their mum or their dad -- and I think I go on to say how beneficial it was for [Baby C] because he did calm down and was well, looked stable on his mum (inaudible).
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Is he able to stay on CPAP when he engages with skinto-skin with mum?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You can take babies out to have skin-to-skin while on CPAP, but in this instance we'd taken him off CPAP and then I think I say further down in my notes that just maybe some facial oxygen if he required it.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Let's carry on with your note then. You're quite right, it carries on:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Taken off CPAP while out having skin-to-skin with mum. Calmed down straightaway while on mummy. Just required some facial O2 while out."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: O2 is oxygen?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Oxygen.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Thank you:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "No signs of increased work of breathing."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Just tell us a little bit about that, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is that something you'd have been looking out for?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Absolutely, always we make sure with the respiratory rates, any recession, that if the baby's working particularly harder, then that can be a sign that they obviously need respiratory support.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: So are we talking now of a period that [Baby C]'s been taken off his CPAP?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: He's with mum?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: And you're just keeping an eye on that to make sure that there's no deterioration?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: All right:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Weaned off for 2 hours. Again, discussed with reg and decided to try Optiflow in view of [Baby C] being so unsettled on CPAP."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So weaned off what for 2 hours, I suppose, is the first question?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Weaned off CPAP for 2 hours.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: And then another discussion with the registrar?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: And Optiflow, please. What's the difference with Optiflow? What does that tell you about [Baby C]'s condition?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's a less invasive respiratory support, Optiflow. So where CPAP has nasal prongs that are quite invasive and quite uncomfortable, Optiflow is less invasive, more comfortable for babies.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Right:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Optiflow commenced [or commenced Optiflow] at 13.00 hours with flow of 6 litres in 23-28% oxygen.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Very settled this afternoon. Slight increase in respiratory rate but..."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Respirations", is that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: "... remain between 60 to 70 per minute."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Breaths per minute, yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: "Heart rate stable at 150 and temp within normal limits."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So what, if anything, as his designated nurse, do you take from those various observations?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That he was stable.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: "CBG taken after 2 hours. Satisfactory but not quite as good as previous CBG, but similar to CBGs during the night with pH 7.27 and PCO2 7.02."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Could you explain that to us please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I've documented there to say that the capillary blood gas wasn't as good as it had been in the morning, obviously he'd had 2 hours off nasal CPAP without any respiratory support, and then he had been commenced on Optiflow. So that was just something to be taken into consideration.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Okay. Any alarm at that point?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, because he said -- I've carried on and said, "Clinically remained stable".
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Okay:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Shown to registrar and for repeat at 6 pm."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And then you have made the note:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Clinically remains stable..."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: "... but aware do not want to push [Baby C]."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Could you just explain that observation, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Again, with any baby, you would be making sure that you're looking at the work of breathing, making sure -obviously because we had stepped him down to Optiflow, that he wasn't in any way struggling.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: "Bloods taken at 15.00 hours. Platelets improved slightly to 49 today. Still not for LP at present."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We heard yesterday about platelets and LP stands for lumbar puncture. Could you tell us anything about that entry that occurred to you at the time?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, other than, obviously, a lumbar puncture is very invasive and so it would have been quite stressful for [Baby C], so it's just balancing out those risks.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: "Fluids increased to 120ml per kilogram per day. Lipid increased and 10% dextrose discontinued."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: What's the significance of those entries, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Fluids were increased because he would have been day 4, so every day the fluids, in mils ml per kilo, goes up, it increases up to day 5 usually. The 10% dextrose stops. We use 10% dextrose as an extra if -- depending what day the baby is on fluids-wise. So with the increase of lipids, because it's day 4, the 10% dextrose wouldn't be needed.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Just remind us, please, what lipids are in summary?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You have got your total parenteral nutrition, which is standard, but lipid is fat, so it supports you nutritionally for babies. And that is given via a central line; it can't be administered via a peripheral line, such as a cannula.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: So it's something that's additional to the TPN?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Absolutely, supports nutrition.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Okay:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Continues to have dark bile aspirates. Frequently this morning but improving this afternoon."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So tell us please about dark bile aspirates. We've heard what an aspirate is. What's the significance, or otherwise, of a dark bile?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's not reassuring to have dark bile aspirates because obviously it could indicate conditions such as necrotising enterocolitis, NEC as it's known as, so that's obviously something to monitor.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: So you are aspirating the tube into his stomach, you're getting -- let me just -- dark bile aspirates --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: -- of concern?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, any aspirated dark bile would be a concern.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Escalated to anybody, do you remember?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, yes, the registrar.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Who did you discuss that with?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The registrar and I believe I discussed it with Dr Gibbs.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Who is Dr Gibbs, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The consultant paediatrician.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Right. Was he on duty that day?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Right. Do you remember what view was taken, as far as you were concerned, on what treatment you were recommended as a consequence of escalating that to the registrar and Dr Gibbs?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Obviously, we would always escalate it to the medical staff and we wouldn't -- we would be concerned about feeding him. He would have been on a cautious feeding regime anyway and he was nil by mouth.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Okay. Now:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Passed NGT as [Baby C] pulled out."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Just explain that to us, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's me passing a tube. He did have an orogastric tube, which is obviously in his mouth. I passed one down his nose. It's actually less -- it's more comforting for a baby because, as you can imagine, a tube in your mouth can be quite invasive so we passed a nasogastric tube.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Do you remember roughly when that was during the course of your shift?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No. Um -- no.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Okay. It goes on to say:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Two OGTs this morning whilst upset."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Because he was fractious, so as you can imagine, he was lovely and feisty, so he would just pull them out, and they're quite easy to pull out from your mouth. All they need to do is use their little fingers and they're pulled out.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Do you remember what sort of period of the shift those two events took place (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I've said that they -- "Pulled out two OGs this morning", so in the morning.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Was it after those two oral tubes that you decided to go for the nasal option?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't recall.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: You can't recall? All right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "NGT on free drainage."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Why would an NGT be on free drainage, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Because if they're not being fed and, again, we use it in CPAP and we use it in Optiflow, if we think that the babies maybe are quite gaseous then we can leave it on free drainage to stop any accumulation of air.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And also to see any aspirate, bile aspirates coming back.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: We've been told how this tube enters either, in [Baby C]'s case, earlier in your shift orally --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: -- or nasally --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: -- and obviously that the tip is inside the baby. Just tell us a bit more about free drainage, what does that involve?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It can be -- we can use a little bag that we can have attached to it or we can use an open-ended syringe.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Okay. If it's not on free drainage what's the situation with your end of the tube?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It would be -- it's a connector, so it's just connected off.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Okay. So connected off means closed?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Closed, yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Free drainage means presumably?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Open.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: All right, thanks. Just so we understand.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: What's the purpose of leaving it on free drainage again?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Again, to reduce any air build-up that might be in the stomach or any aspirates.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Okay. During the course of your handover that morning was anything brought to your attention that was concerning in the stomach?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I would have assumed that it would have been if there was concerns prior to because we get a comprehensive handover.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: That's just the type of thing, is it, that would be discussed on handover?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Absolutely.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: All right. So free drainage would allow, presumably, air to escape, but also I think you mentioned aspirates.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You tell me what the effect of free drainage is on aspirates, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So -- well, with aspirates, obviously if you were in free drainage bag, which actually at this time potentially he wouldn't have had on -- I believe that it would be an open syringe hung in the incubator, which can let any air expel.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: You were indicating your left arm up there. Perhaps you could just explain this.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So when we have nursed babies on CPAP or Optiflow and we're concerned we want the baby to have free drainage, we attach a syringe, a 10ml syringe, and in the incubator we have what we call an incubator tree, and that can be hung on there and that can just obviously expel any air if we think there is an accumulation.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: So if I'm right, the syringe is actually attached to the end of the --
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Tube.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: -- oral or nasal tube?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Obviously at the open end --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: -- it's left open and any air can then escape that needs to escape?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: And had [Baby C] had problems with air in his tummy the day before, that's just the type of thing you think would have been brought to your attention on the handover?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: "Abdo full but soft."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: What's the significance or not of that, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Because they're preterm babies, obviously we're all the time making checks to make sure what their abdomen appears to be. And in this case I've put that it appears full, but it's soft to touch on examination.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Okay. What, if anything does, that tell you?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That it's quite normal for a baby, for [Baby C].
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Okay. It says:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Slight shine to abdo but not veiny or over-distended."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That may well speak for itself, but just tell us a little bit what those issues mean.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So indications can be for what I said before, necrotising enterocolitis, NEC as it's called, NEC, what you're looking for is a shiny appearance, the abdomen can look veiny, distended, darkening. These are all signs that could be possible early signs of NEC.

blocks.text: To try it.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: To try it, yes. Just following it through, you've been very clear, you put the detail in and we've got here:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "CBG taken after it 2 hours, satisfactory but not quite as good as previous CBG."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: So that's the blood gas, it's all right but it's not as good?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: It is. I think later on, just whilst we're dealing with blood gas, we'll come back to this section, but just so we have the picture with blood gas, could we just look at the right-hand side of your notes for the entry made a little later? Top right.

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: So improvement but still not bang in the zone you'd like; is that correct?

blocks.text: It obviously -- it's all in relation to his previous ones --
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: -- but obviously I've documented and informed the doctors of that slight rise in lactate.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: That's the thing. It's all relative to the condition that he is in, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's just making sure that everybody's aware.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Can we go back then to where we were, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You've got, right in the centre here:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Shown to registrar [this is after the blood gas].
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: For repeat at 1800."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We've seen that:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Clinically remains stable but aware do not want to push [Baby C]."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That was your assessment at this point, isn't it, Mrs Williams?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: And that reflects your caution, clinically, in how to deal with [Baby C] at this point, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, it's making sure that clinically we're doing individualised care and recognising that we are very aware of what is happening with [Baby C] and what he needs.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: When you say not to push [Baby C], what sort of thing do you mean would push [Baby C]?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Obviously, tire [Baby C].
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Tire him.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's why we're always mindful with the LP, the lumbar puncture, not to be performing things.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: We're going to see later as we go on there's a question as to when feeds might start is [Baby C]. Is that the sort of thing to bear in terms of not pushing, that you don't give a baby like this feeds if there could be problems that the feeds could create?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, but in this context I feel I've documented it in respiratory --
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: You're thinking about respiratory there. It could apply to feeding, couldn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, that's why he would be on a cautious feeding regime because of the risks that he's got.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: So it could apply to feeding then?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: (Inaudible).
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: I can't tell --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Remained stable but aware do not want to push [Baby C]."
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: I said I feel I put that in the context of his respiratory, not for feeding.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: I know you have done that, Mrs Williams, but I'm just asking, could that apply to feeding as well?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Thank you. If we move on:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Bloods taken at 15.00. Platelets improved slightly to 49 today."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: But we've heard platelets, the aim would be for them to be about 100 to 150, something like that, wouldn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: And 49 is still pretty low, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: So in terms of signs that -- whether or not that's causing a problem in itself, it's not a good sign if they're that low, is it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Then we've got:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Continues to have dark bile aspirates."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And you've been quite clear that's always going to be a matter of concern, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: And we've seen from the charts that there'd been aspirates being produced during the day, hadn't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: And we understand it had begun the day before.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Carrying on, we've got:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "NGT on free drainage."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So it's the next paragraph. You explained what that is:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Abdo full but soft. Slight shine to abdo but not veiny or overdistended."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'd just like us to be clear exactly what that means, why you have recorded it.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: As previously said, what we would be looking for is any signs, early signs of NEC. So I have said that there is a slight shine, so that's something to be aware of. But however it's not veiny or distended, which are signs of necrotising enterocolitis.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: So there might be different stages the presentation might go through and that's what you're looking for?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, and it can be different in different babies.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Sorry, you said "which are signs of" and then you dropped your voice and I couldn't hear what you said.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Of NEC.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Thank you. I thought it was, but I just wanted to check.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: And indeed, NEC, because of [Baby C]'s condition, is something that was on your mind but indeed there might be any number of abdominal or stomach complaints that could present themselves with a stomach distending?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Do you agree?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Stomach distension can be masqueraded in other conditions, yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: That's right. You had NEC in mind because that was a particular concern with [Baby C], that's right, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's a concern for any preterm baby.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Yes, it is. But there are other things, other problems, that could cause an abdomen to distend, aren't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, but, however, NEC (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: NEC is the one you're talking of.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: [Baby C] had not received anything -- he'd been nil by mouth to this point; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: From my notes, yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: We know that there were fluids he was receiving?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Looking at the overall picture, after veiny or overdistended, you have got "BNO", which is bowels not opened, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: So that means that, even with the NGT on free drainage, so excess air could come out, his abdomen is still swelling as we go along, or has swollen a bit as we got along, hasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I've not -- I've said it's not over-distended, it just looks full.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Just full. But nothing has yet passed through him and come out, has it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: On my shift. I don't know about if they'd had bowels open. We document on shifts --
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: No, we haven't. So this is 3 days in?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: And bowels still not open?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And he hadn't been fed.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Yes, he hadn't been fed. Now, you have put it aspirates.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "If aspirates improve, can start trophic feeds this evening."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And by trophic, you explained, that means being fed with milk through the tube?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, and it'd be expressed breast milk because mum had already started that process of expressing. And they would only be -- again, it would be referring to the cautious feeding guidelines that we have, which might be 0.5ml twelve-hourly.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: But that's dependent on the aspirates improving?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, and the overall clinical picture.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: And the overall clinical picture. Because it may not be ideal to give him milk of whatever volume if there's a problem developing in his abdomen as demonstrated by the aspirates; do you agree?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: What's difficult is you have to clinically make that judgment, which the doctors would do, to make sure that obviously digestion and that his gut is preserved and that's -sometimes they are given small amounts of trophic feed to make that gut start up.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: A lot of these matters turn sometimes on quite delicate issues of clinical judgment, don't they? You're nodding.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, sorry, yes. And individual care.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: And individual care. We can just see the last entry here on this side:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Weighed today in incubator without CPAP and current weight 717 grams."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So 84 grams lost?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: As you said and as people may know, one expects a baby to lose some weight in the period soon after birth. In a baby whose starting point is 800 grams going down to 717 is of itself not good, is it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's expected to lose weight.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: But was there a -- it's expected to, but relative to the size of the baby in the first place it's quite a significant reduction, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think it all has to be taken into the context of different scales used when the baby was born. Obviously I've removed all the -- obviously CPAP but the baby would have lines, it had a long line, so...
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: But there's a clinical balance here between -- you see, the desire to get feeds going in as against the situation with the aspirates, isn't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. But that's why it's so important to have TPN and lipids for nutrition.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: Yes. I'm just going to ask you, if you look across to the right-hand side, and it's the last part of the note.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If we can just enlarge the top right.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You have put -- just the last couple of lines on the top note:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Remains stable on Optiflow. BP stable."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Is that blood pressure?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: "Aspirates reduced this evening [question] commence enteral feed tonight."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Is that right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Query query."
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: As in do we, should we --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. That's on the radar. That would be the -- that's ideally the plan to commence feeds.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: And that depends, in your view, on the notes you're putting there, as to the situation, amongst other things, with the aspirate?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. It's:
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: "[Query query] commence enteral feeds tonight depending on [Baby C]'s condition and medical" --
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMS

blocks.text: All right. Thank you, Mrs Williams. That's what I wanted to ask.
